Maladaptive Strategies.value: Making any plans for the future
try hard not think about the trauma
keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: The profile is for trauma to a loved one, but the threat items are dominated by direct personal pursuit/attack themes (someone following me, needing to check immediate personal safety, planning escape routes). That pattern fits interpersonal victimization of the self more than bereavement/trauma-to-loved-one and is hard to reconcile without any corresponding memory content about being personally endangered.

issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, Threat and Memory are tightly linked, yet the memory items are about guilt, emotional overwhelm, and patchy recall, while the threat items are about current physical surveillance/attack. There is little plausible content connection between these selected memory items and the very specific threat behaviors, so the strong Threat ↔ Memory pattern is not well reflected.

issues.item: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: Revenge fantasies toward those responsible can occur after a loved one is harmed, but paired with checking behind, waking to check safety, and escape-route planning, the overall pattern implies ongoing direct threat to the patient rather than distress centered on the loved one's trauma. This cross-node combination is clinically difficult to explain as one coherent presentation from the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: These threat and safety-behaviour items imply an ongoing interpersonal pursuit or direct personal danger to the patient. That is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of trauma to a loved one, unless there is additional unreported threat to self.

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: The profile otherwise centres on guilt, emotional overwhelm, and fragmented recall linked to the loved one's trauma, which fits bereavement/indirect trauma. Escape-route planning and checking if someone is following him pull toward a different trauma context and are not well integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, revenge fantasies can be plausible if there is an identifiable perpetrator, but here the rest of the profile does not establish an assault/perpetrator context. In the absence of any trigger, memory, or appraisal content about attackers or blame, this item is hard to integrate clinically with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: The threat items are specifically about the patient checking whether he himself is physically safe at night. For trauma to a loved one, this can occur, but in this profile there are no triggers or appraisals supporting a persistent personal-danger formulation. The memory items centre on guilt and emotional overwhelm about the event, making the nocturnal self-protection theme feel disconnected.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: The Threat node is internally strained by combining general negative emotions and generic sleep problems with a highly specific hypervigilance item ('need to stay alert'). For a trauma involving harm to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing immediate-danger posture toward the patient's own safety that is not supported by the memory content, appraisals, or strategies provided. The rest of the profile is dominated by guilt, overwhelming recall, patchy memory, suppression, and distraction, which coheres with trauma to a loved one and severe PTSD, but does not clinically anchor a strong 'must stay alert' threat theme. This makes the sleep-vigilance item the main incoherent selection relative to the rest of the formulation and profile.

vignette:
Martin Keller is a 49-year-old fashion designer who came to treatment nearly a year after his wife was struck by a car while crossing a street outside his studio. He had been walking a few steps behind her at the end of a long workday, distracted by garment notes on his phone, when he looked up to the sound of brakes and saw her thrown sideways onto the pavement. What remained with him was not a complete story but a series of brutally sharp fragments: the angle of her body under the streetlight, one of her shoes in the road, the sound he made when he reached her. Around those moments there were blanks he could not fill in. He could not clearly reconstruct who called 911, what the bystanders said, or how he got to the hospital. When the memory came back, it did so unevenly and with punishing force, and Martin was seized by the conviction that he should have been paying attention, should have stopped her, should have done something different.

In the first weeks after she survived the accident and began a long physical recovery, Martin found that remembering any part of that night could undo him. If an image surfaced, he was suddenly flooded with guilt and a level of emotion so intense he had to stop whatever he was doing. In client meetings he would lose track of a conversation; in the studio, while reviewing fabrics under bright track lighting that reminded him of the street scene, his chest would tighten and his hands would shake. Because the memory was both fragmented and unbearable, he started working hard not to let it form at all. He kept podcasts playing in the car, answered emails late into the night, and filled every spare moment with sketching or scrolling supplier lists, anything to keep his mind occupied. He also stopped making plans beyond the immediate week. Looking ahead to a vacation, a show, even dinner next month felt intolerable, as though the future itself had become unsafe and presumptuous.

Those efforts did not settle him. Martin lived in a state of strain marked by fear, anger, guilt, and shame that seemed to flare without warning. He slept badly, lying awake replaying flashes he did not want and then jolting up if he did drift off. At work he began avoiding the window facing the crosswalk outside the building, and if he heard tires screech in the street during a fitting, he felt a hot rush through his body before he could think. The strength of those reactions made him even more determined to push the whole event out of mind. He told himself that if he could stay busy enough and refuse to think about it, he might keep from falling apart in front of his staff or his wife.

Instead, the more threatened he felt, the less room there was in his mind for anything but fragments. Exhausted by poor sleep and constantly braced for reminders, he found that the memory returned in the same jagged form: a few crystal-clear seconds surrounded by emptiness, followed immediately by crushing guilt. He would begin to recall the accident and then shut it down almost at once, turning back to work, opening another tab on his laptop, asking an assistant for an unnecessary revision. That habit of cutting the memory off left it unchanged, still sharp where it was sharp and blank where it was blank, so that the next reminder hit with the same force. In recent months this has narrowed his life considerably. His wife has noticed that he refuses to talk about future plans for her continued rehabilitation or for their anniversary, and he gives vague answers when she asks what he wants six months from now. In the studio he remains productive in a driven, brittle way, but colleagues have commented that he never stops moving and seems unable to tolerate quiet.

By the time he sought help, Martin was frightened by how trapped he felt between the memory and his efforts to escape it. He could see that his constant distraction and refusal to think ahead were not giving him relief for more than a few minutes, yet he was afraid that if he let himself remember fully, he would be overwhelmed by guilt and emotion he could not control. What brought him in was a recent moment at work when the squeal of brakes outside his showroom left him shaking so visibly that a junior designer asked if he needed an ambulance. Martin said he wants to sleep, to stop living as if disaster is about to happen again, and most of all to find some way to remember what happened to his wife without feeling that the memory proves he failed her.
